claim: Gut microbial metabolism is associated with host longevity.
source: Gut microbial metabolism is associated with host longevity.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a general assertion about the relationship between gut microbial metabolism and host longevity, supported by citations in the introduction.

claim: Establishing a causal link between gut microbial metabolism and host longevity requires direct manipulation of microbial metabolism in situ.
source: However, because it requires direct manipulation of microbial metabolism in situ, establishing a causal link between these two processes remains challenging.
evidence: This is a methodological assertion about what is required to establish causality, based on scientific reasoning about experimental requirements.

claim: An optogenetic method can control gene expression and metabolite production from bacteria residing in the host gut.
source: We demonstrate an optogenetic method to control gene expression and metabolite production from bacteria residing in the host gut.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented throughout the manuscript, including Figures 1-4.

claim: An E. coli strain can be genetically engineered to secrete colanic acid under the quantitative control of light.
source: We genetically engineer an Escherichia coli strain that secretes colanic acid (CA) under the quantitative control of light.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing light-controlled CA production in Figure 2.

claim: Colanic acid produced in the C. elegans gut protects intestinal mitochondria from stress-induced hyper-fragmentation.
source: Using this optogenetically-controlled strain to induce CA production directly in the Caenorhabditis elegans gut, we reveal the local effect of CA in protecting intestinal mitochondria from stress-induced hyper-fragmentation.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data in Figure 3 showing mitochondrial morphology changes.

claim: The lifespan-extending effect of the optogenetically-controlled strain is positively correlated with the intensity of green light.
source: We also demonstrate that the lifespan-extending effect of this strain is positively correlated with the intensity of green light, indicating a dose-dependent CA benefit on the host.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data in Figure 4b showing dose-dependent lifespan extension.

claim: Optogenetics can achieve quantitative and temporal control of gut bacterial metabolism to reveal local and systemic effects on host health and aging.
source: Thus, optogenetics can be used to achieve quantitative and temporal control of gut bacterial metabolism in order to reveal its local and systemic effects on host health and aging.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data presented throughout the manuscript.

claim: 16S rRNA and metagenomic DNA sequencing are used to associate the presence or abundance of specific bacteria to human centenarians.
source: For example, 16S rRNA and metagenomic DNA sequencing are used to associate the presence or abundance of specific bacteria to human centenarians (Biagi et al., 2016; Claesson et al., 2012; Claesson et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: 16S rRNA and metagenomic DNA sequencing approaches are unable to elucidate how a specific microbial species contributes to longevity given the complexity and heterogeneity of the human gut environment.
source: However, given the complexity and heterogeneity of the human gut environment, these approaches are unable to elucidate how a specific microbial species contributes to longevity.
evidence: This is an inference about the limitations of these methods based on the complexity of the system.

claim: C. elegans has a short and easily-measured lifespan.
source: The nematode Caenorhabditis elegans has a short and easily-measured lifespan, features that have revolutionized our understanding of the molecular genetics of aging and longevity (Kenyon, 2010).
evidence: This is established knowledge about C. elegans as a model organism, supported by citation.

claim: C. elegans has revolutionized our understanding of the molecular genetics of aging and longevity.
source: The nematode Caenorhabditis elegans has a short and easily-measured lifespan, features that have revolutionized our understanding of the molecular genetics of aging and longevity (Kenyon, 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: Studies using C. elegans provide mechanistic insight into the association between bacterial species and host longevity.
source: Studies using C. elegans also provide mechanistic insight into the association between bacterial species and host longevity (Gusarov et al., 2013; Kim, 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Bacterial metabolism can produce specific products to directly influence the aging process in C. elegans.
source: Importantly, recent studies have revealed that bacterial metabolism can produce specific products to directly influence the aging process in the host C. elegans or modulate the effects of environmental cues on C. elegans lifespan (Cabreiro et al., 2013; Pryor et al., 2019; Virk et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Bacterial metabolism can modulate the effects of environmental cues on C. elegans lifespan.
source: Importantly, recent studies have revealed that bacterial metabolism can produce specific products to directly influence the aging process in the host C. elegans or modulate the effects of environmental cues on C. elegans lifespan (Cabreiro et al., 2013; Pryor et al., 2019; Virk et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Bacterial metabolism is significant in regulating host physiology during the aging process.
source: These findings highlight the significance of bacterial metabolism in regulating host physiology during the aging process and have inspired interest in directly manipulating bacterial metabolism in situ in the host gastrointestinal (GI) tract.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the cited studies about bacterial metabolism and aging.

claim: Researchers have administered antibiotic- or carbohydrate-based small molecule inducers to modulate gene expression from gut bacteria.
source: In several recent studies, researchers have administered antibiotic- or carbohydrate-based small molecule inducers to modulate gene expression from gut bacteria (Kotula et al., 2014; Lim et al., 2017; Mimee et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Chemical effectors may have unwanted side-effects on host or microbial physiology.
source: While this approach can be used to perform in situ analyses of gut bacterial-host interactions (Lim et al., 2017), chemical effectors may have unwanted side-effects on host or microbial physiology and are subject to slow and poorly-controlled transport and degradation processes that ultimately limit their precision.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about potential limitations of chemical inducers based on general knowledge of their properties.

claim: Chemical effectors are subject to slow and poorly-controlled transport and degradation processes that limit their precision.
source: While this approach can be used to perform in situ analyses of gut bacterial-host interactions (Lim et al., 2017), chemical effectors may have unwanted side-effects on host or microbial physiology and are subject to slow and poorly-controlled transport and degradation processes that ultimately limit their precision.
evidence: This is based on general knowledge about the behavior of chemical inducers in biological systems.

claim: Optogenetics combines light and genetically-engineered photoreceptors to enable control of biological processes.
source: Optogenetics combines light and genetically-engineered photoreceptors to enable unrivaled control of biological processes (Olson and Tabor, 2014).
evidence: This is established knowledge about optogenetics, supported by citation.

claim: Photoreceptors have been engineered that regulate bacterial gene expression in response to specific wavelengths of light.
source: Previously, we and others have engineered photoreceptors that regulate bacterial gene expression in response to specific wavelengths of light (Levskaya et al., 2005; Li et al., 2020; Ohlendorf et al., 2012; Ong and Tabor, 2018; Ong et al., 2018; Ramakrishnan and Tabor, 2016; Ryu and Gomelsky, 2014; Schmidl et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Photoreceptors have been used to achieve precise quantitative control of bacterial gene expression in in vitro culture conditions.
source: These photoreceptors have been used to achieve precise quantitative (Olson et al., 2017; Olson et al., 2014), temporal (Chait et al., 2017; Milias-Argeitis et al., 2016; Olson et al., 2017; Olson et al., 2014), and spatial (Chait et al., 2017; Levskaya et al., 2005; Ohlendorf et al., 2012; Tabor et al., 2011) control of bacterial gene expression in in vitro culture conditions.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Photoreceptors have been used to achieve precise temporal control of bacterial gene expression in in vitro culture conditions.
source: These photoreceptors have been used to achieve precise quantitative (Olson et al., 2017; Olson et al., 2014), temporal (Chait et al., 2017; Milias-Argeitis et al., 2016; Olson et al., 2017; Olson et al., 2014), and spatial (Chait et al., 2017; Levskaya et al., 2005; Ohlendorf et al., 2012; Tabor et al., 2011) control of bacterial gene expression in in vitro culture conditions.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Photoreceptors have been used to achieve precise spatial control of bacterial gene expression in in vitro culture conditions.
source: These photoreceptors have been used to achieve precise quantitative (Olson et al., 2017; Olson et al., 2014), temporal (Chait et al., 2017; Milias-Argeitis et al., 2016; Olson et al., 2017; Olson et al., 2014), and spatial (Chait et al., 2017; Levskaya et al., 2005; Ohlendorf et al., 2012; Tabor et al., 2011) control of bacterial gene expression in in vitro culture conditions.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Photoreceptors have been used to characterize and control transcriptional regulatory circuits.
source: They have also been used to characterize and control transcriptional regulatory circuits (Chait et al., 2017; Olson et al., 2014; Tabor et al., 2009) and bacterial metabolic pathways (Fernandez-Rodriguez et al., 2017; Tandar et al., 2019) in vitro.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Photoreceptors have been used to characterize and control bacterial metabolic pathways in vitro.
source: They have also been used to characterize and control transcriptional regulatory circuits (Chait et al., 2017; Olson et al., 2014; Tabor et al., 2009) and bacterial metabolic pathways (Fernandez-Rodriguez et al., 2017; Tandar et al., 2019) in vitro.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The E. coli and C. elegans interaction model is an optically transparent system with known mechanistic links between bacterial metabolism and host longevity.
source: We address this possibility using the E. coli and C. elegans interaction model, an optically transparent system with known mechanistic links between bacterial metabolism and host longevity.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge about these model organisms and their interactions.

claim: Colanic acid is an exopolysaccharide synthesized and secreted by E. coli.
source: In particular, CA is an exopolysaccharide synthesized and secreted by E. coli that can extend the lifespan of the host C. elegans by modulating mitochondrial dynamics (Han et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: Colanic acid can extend the lifespan of C. elegans by modulating mitochondrial dynamics.
source: In particular, CA is an exopolysaccharide synthesized and secreted by E. coli that can extend the lifespan of the host C. elegans by modulating mitochondrial dynamics (Han et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: E. coli strains can be engineered to express fluorescent reporter proteins under control of the CcaSR two-component system.
source: First, we engineer E. coli strains that express fluorescent reporter proteins under control of our previously engineered green light-activated, red light de-activated two-component system CcaSR (Schmidl et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data in Figure 1 and citation to previous work.

claim: CcaSR is a green light-activated, red light de-activated two-component system.
source: First, we engineer E. coli strains that express fluorescent reporter proteins under control of our previously engineered green light-activated, red light de-activated two-component system CcaSR (Schmidl et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work and experimental data in Figure 1.

claim: Worms carrying engineered E. coli in their GI tracts can be exposed to time-varying green and red light signals to demonstrate optical activation and de-activation of bacterial gene expression in worm gut.
source: We then expose worms carrying these engineered E. coli in their GI tracts to time-varying green and red light signals to demonstrate optical activation and de-activation of bacterial gene expression in worm gut.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data in Figure 1.

claim: Green light-induced CA from bacteria residing in the host gut is sufficient to modulate mitochondrial dynamics and lifespan.
source: Our experiments reveal that green light-induced CA from bacteria residing in the host gut is sufficient to modulate mitochondrial dynamics and lifespan.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data in Figures 3 and 4.

claim: In strain LH01, green light-exposure switches CcaS to an active state in the presence of chromophore phycocyanobilin (PCB).
source: In LH01, green light-exposure switches CcaS to an active state in the presence of chromophore phycocyanobilin (PCB), wherein it phosphorylates the response regulator CcaR.
evidence: This is based on the known mechanism of CcaSR and experimental data showing light-dependent responses.

claim: Active CcaS phosphorylates the response regulator CcaR.
source: In LH01, green light-exposure switches CcaS to an active state in the presence of chromophore phycocyanobilin (PCB), wherein it phosphorylates the response regulator CcaR.
evidence: This is based on the known mechanism of two-component systems and CcaSR specifically.

claim: Phosphorylated CcaR activates transcription of sfgfp from the PcpcG2-172 output promoter.
source: Phosphorylated CcaR then activates transcription of sfgfp from the PcpcG2-172 output promoter.
evidence: This is based on the known mechanism of CcaSR and experimental data showing light-dependent sfGFP expression.

claim: Red light reverts active CcaS to the inactive form, de-activating sfgfp expression.
source: Red light reverts active CcaS to the inactive form, de-activating sfgfp expression (Figure 1a).
evidence: This is based on the known mechanism of CcaSR and experimental data showing light-dependent responses.

claim: In the step ON experiment, sfGFP fluorescence in the worm gut lumen starts low, begins to increase within 2 hr, and reaches a saturated high level at 6 hr.
source: In the step ON experiment, sfGFP fluorescence in the worm gut lumen starts low, begins to increase within 2 hr, and reaches a saturated high level at 6 hr (Figure 1d).
evidence: This is directly supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1d.

claim: In the step OFF experiment, sfGFP fluorescence begins high, and decreases exponentially between hours 1–7.
source: On the other hand, in the step OFF experiment, sfGFP fluorescence begins high, and decreases exponentially between hours 1–7 (Figure 1d).
evidence: This is directly supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1d.

claim: The light response is abolished when the PCB biosynthetic operon is removed (ΔPCB).
source: This light response is abolished when the PCB biosynthetic operon is removed (ΔPCB) (Figure 1d), demonstrating that changes in sfGFP fluorescence are due to CcaSR photoswitching in the worm gut.
evidence: This is directly supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1d.

claim: Changes in sfGFP fluorescence are due to CcaSR photoswitching in the worm gut.
source: This light response is abolished when the PCB biosynthetic operon is removed (ΔPCB) (Figure 1d), demonstrating that changes in sfGFP fluorescence are due to CcaSR photoswitching in the worm gut.
evidence: This is an inference from the ΔPCB control experiment showing that the response requires the PCB chromophore.

claim: Engineered bacteria remain intact in the host gut.
source: We observed that our engineered bacteria remain intact in the host gut (Figure 1—figure supplement 2) and respond to light in a unimodal fashion (Figure 1e–g).
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: Engineered bacteria in the host gut respond to light in a unimodal fashion.
source: We observed that our engineered bacteria remain intact in the host gut (Figure 1—figure supplement 2) and respond to light in a unimodal fashion (Figure 1e–g).
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figures 1e-g.

claim: The temporal dynamics and PCB dependence of the gene expression responses measured by flow cytometry recapitulate the microscopy results.
source: The temporal dynamics and PCB dependence of the gene expression responses recapitulate the microscopy results (Figure 1—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is supported by comparison of data in Figure 1d and Figure 1—figure supplement 3.

claim: Residual bacteria on the exterior of worms do not contribute to the flow cytometry measurements.
source: We also confirmed that residual bacteria on the exterior of worms do not contribute to the flow cytometry measurements (Figure 1—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This is supported by control experiments shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 4.

claim: Optogenetics can be used to rapidly and reversibly induce gene expression of E. coli residing in the C. elegans gut.
source: Together, these microscopy and flow cytometry experiments demonstrate that we can use optogenetics to rapidly and reversibly induce gene expression of E. coli residing in the C. elegans gut.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data in Figure 1.

claim: Bacterial genes involved in the same metabolic process are often clustered into operons and co-regulated at the transcriptional level.
source: Bacterial genes involved in the same metabolic process are often clustered into operons and co-regulated at the transcriptional level.
evidence: This is established knowledge about bacterial gene organization.

claim: The cps operon in E. coli consists of 19 genes that encode enzymes required for the biosynthesis and secretion of CA.
source: The cps operon in E. coli consists of 19 genes that encode enzymes required for the biosynthesis and secretion of CA (Torres-Cabassa and Gottesman, 1987), and CA-overproducing bacterial mutants Δlon and Δhns promote longevity in the host C. elegans (Han et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: CA-overproducing bacterial mutants Δlon and Δhns promote longevity in the host C. elegans.
source: The cps operon in E. coli consists of 19 genes that encode enzymes required for the biosynthesis and secretion of CA (Torres-Cabassa and Gottesman, 1987), and CA-overproducing bacterial mutants Δlon and Δhns promote longevity in the host C. elegans (Han et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: Strain MVK29 lacks genomic rcsA and expresses a heterologous copy of rcsA under the control of CcaSR.
source: To place CA biosynthesis under optogenetic control, we engineered E. coli strain MVK29 which lacks genomic rcsA, and expresses a heterologous copy of rcsA under the control of CcaSR (Figure 2a, Supplementary file 1a, 1b).
evidence: This is a description of the genetic engineering performed, supported by Figure 2a.

claim: In red light, MVK29 secretes CA to concentrations below the limit of detection of the assay, similar to the ΔrcsA mutant.
source: In red light, MVK29 secretes CA to concentrations below the limit of detection of the assay, similar to the ΔrcsA mutant (Figure 2b).
evidence: This is directly supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2b.

claim: Green light induces MVK29 to secrete high levels of CA.
source: Green light, on the other hand, induces MVK29 to secrete high levels of CA, and removal of the PCB biosynthetic operon abolishes this response (Figure 2b).
evidence: This is directly supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2b.

claim: Removal of the PCB biosynthetic operon abolishes the green light-induced CA secretion response in MVK29.
source: Green light, on the other hand, induces MVK29 to secrete high levels of CA, and removal of the PCB biosynthetic operon abolishes this response (Figure 2b).
evidence: This is directly supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2b.

claim: Mutation of the CcaS catalytic histidine to a non-functional alanine (H534A) abolishes detectable CA production.
source: Moreover, mutation of the CcaS catalytic histidine to a non-functional alanine (H534A), or the CcaR phosphorylation site from an aspartic acid to a non-functional asparagine (D51N) abolishes detectable CA production (Figure 2b).
evidence: This is directly supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2b.

claim: Mutation of the CcaR phosphorylation site from an aspartic acid to a non-functional asparagine (D51N) abolishes detectable CA production.
source: Moreover, mutation of the CcaS catalytic histidine to a non-functional alanine (H534A), or the CcaR phosphorylation site from an aspartic acid to a non-functional asparagine (D51N) abolishes detectable CA production (Figure 2b).
evidence: This is directly supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2b.

claim: The level of secreted CA increases sigmoidally with the increasing intensity of green light.
source: Importantly, the level of secreted CA increases sigmoidally with the increasing intensity of green light (Figure 2c), which is consistent with the response of CcaSR (Schmidl et al., 2014).
evidence: This is directly supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2c.

claim: The sigmoidal increase in CA secretion with green light intensity is consistent with the response of CcaSR.
source: Importantly, the level of secreted CA increases sigmoidally with the increasing intensity of green light (Figure 2c), which is consistent with the response of CcaSR (Schmidl et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by comparison to previous characterization of CcaSR cited in the text.

claim: CA production has been placed under the control of CcaSR.
source: We conclude that we have placed CA production under the control of CcaSR, and that we can use light to tune the biosynthesis and secretion of bacterial metabolites.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data in Figure 2.

claim: Light can be used to tune the biosynthesis and secretion of bacterial metabolites.
source: We conclude that we have placed CA production under the control of CcaSR, and that we can use light to tune the biosynthesis and secretion of bacterial metabolites.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data in Figure 2 showing dose-dependent CA production.

claim: Lon is an ATP-dependent protease that degrades RcsA.
source: Lon is an ATP-dependent protease that degrades RcsA, and its deletion mutant Δlon shows increased CA production (Han et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: The Δlon deletion mutant shows increased CA production.
source: Lon is an ATP-dependent protease that degrades RcsA, and its deletion mutant Δlon shows increased CA production (Han et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: When grown on Δlon mutant bacteria, worms exhibit elevated mitochondrial fragmentation in intestinal cells, similar to worms with CA supplementation.
source: When grown on Δlon mutant bacteria, worms exhibit elevated mitochondrial fragmentation in intestinal cells, similar to worms with CA supplementation (Han et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: Green light increases mitochondrial fragmentation in MVK29-fed worms.
source: We found that green light increases mitochondrial fragmentation in MVK29-fed worms, but not in worms fed a MVK29 ΔPCB control strain that does not respond to light (Figure 3c, Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is directly supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3c.

claim: Green light does not increase mitochondrial fragmentation in worms fed a MVK29 ΔPCB control strain that does not respond to light.
source: We found that green light increases mitochondrial fragmentation in MVK29-fed worms, but not in worms fed a MVK29 ΔPCB control strain that does not respond to light (Figure 3c, Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is directly supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3c.

claim: The light-inducible CA biosynthetic strain recapitulates the effect of the Δlon mutant or purified CA on the host.
source: Thus, our light-inducible CA biosynthetic strain recapitulates the effect of the Δlon mutant or purified CA on the host.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from comparing the experimental results to previous work with Δlon and purified CA.

claim: 6 hr of levamisole treatment does not kill worms but leads to mitochondrial hyper-fragmentation in the intestine.
source: Unexpectedly, we found that 6 hr of levamisole treatment does not kill worms but leads to mitochondrial hyper-fragmentation in the intestine (Figure 3c,e), possibly due to the inhibitory effect of levamisole on mitochondrial NADH-oxidizing enzymes (Köhler and Bachmann, 1978) and its associated mitochondrial stress.
evidence: This is directly supported by experimental data shown in Figures 3c and 3e.

claim: Levamisole-induced mitochondrial hyper-fragmentation is possibly due to the inhibitory effect of levamisole on mitochondrial NADH-oxidizing enzymes and its associated mitochondrial stress.
source: Unexpectedly, we found that 6 hr of levamisole treatment does not kill worms but leads to mitochondrial hyper-fragmentation in the intestine (Figure 3c,e), possibly due to the inhibitory effect of levamisole on mitochondrial NADH-oxidizing enzymes (Köhler and Bachmann, 1978) and its associated mitochondrial stress.
evidence: This is a speculative explanation supported by citation to previous work on levamisole's effects.

claim: Levamisole-induced mitochondrial hyper-fragmentation was not observed in worms treated with levamisole less than 1 hr.
source: This hyper-fragmentation phenotype was not observed in worms treated with levamisole less than 1 hr.
evidence: This is an observation from the experiments, though the specific data is not shown in a figure.

claim: Stress-induced mitochondrial fragmentation resembles mitochondrial changes related to aging and age-related neurodegenerative diseases.
source: This stress-induced fragmentation resembles mitochondrial changes related to aging and age-related neurodegenerative diseases (Cho et al., 2009; Exner et al., 2007; Sebastián et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Green light exposure suppresses stress-induced hyperfragmentation in paralyzed worms bearing MVK29 in the gut.
source: Interestingly, we found that green light exposure suppresses stress-induced hyperfragmentation in paralyzed worms bearing MVK29 in the gut (Figure 3e, Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is directly supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3e.

claim: Green light does not suppress stress-induced hyperfragmentation in worms bearing the ΔPCB, CcaS(H534A), CcaR(D51N) or ΔrcsA mutant strains.
source: Importantly, we found no such effects in worms bearing the ΔPCB, CcaS(H534A), CcaR(D51N) or ΔrcsA mutant strains (Figure 3e, Figure 3—figure supplement 1), suggesting that this protective effect is a result of light-induced CA overproduction in the gut.
evidence: This is directly supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3e.

claim: The protective effect on mitochondrial fragmentation is a result of light-induced CA overproduction in the gut.
source: Importantly, we found no such effects in worms bearing the ΔPCB, CcaS(H534A), CcaR(D51N) or ΔrcsA mutant strains (Figure 3e, Figure 3—figure supplement 1), suggesting that this protective effect is a result of light-induced CA overproduction in the gut.
evidence: This is an inference from the control experiments showing that the effect requires functional CcaSR and CA production.

claim: 6 hr levamisole treatment induces mitochondrial hyper-fragmentation in the muscle as it does in the intestine.
source: We found that 6 hr levamisole treatment induces mitochondrial hyper-fragmentation in the muscle as it does in the intestine, but that light-induced CA production from the gut bacteria does not protect muscular mitochondria against hyper-fragmentation (Figure 3f, Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is directly supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3f.

claim: Light-induced CA production from the gut bacteria does not protect muscular mitochondria against hyper-fragmentation.
source: We found that 6 hr levamisole treatment induces mitochondrial hyper-fragmentation in the muscle as it does in the intestine, but that light-induced CA production from the gut bacteria does not protect muscular mitochondria against hyper-fragmentation (Figure 3f, Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is directly supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3f.

claim: Optogenetics can be utilized to induce CA secretion from gut-borne E. coli in vivo.
source: These results not only show that optogenetics can be utilized to induce CA secretion from gut-borne E. coli in vivo, but also reveal a local protective effect of CA on intestinal cells.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data in Figure 3.

claim: CA has a local protective effect on intestinal cells.
source: These results not only show that optogenetics can be utilized to induce CA secretion from gut-borne E. coli in vivo, but also reveal a local protective effect of CA on intestinal cells.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data showing protection in intestinal but not muscle cells.

claim: Green-light-exposed MVK29 can induce CA overproduction to a level comparable to the Δlon mutant.
source: We first confirmed that green-light-exposed MVK29 can induce CA overproduction to a level comparable to the Δlon mutant (Figure 4a, Figure 4—figure supplement 1), and neither the Δlon nor the ΔrcsA mutant responds to light (Figure 4a).
evidence: This is directly supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4a.

claim: Neither the Δlon nor the ΔrcsA mutant responds to light.
source: We first confirmed that green-light-exposed MVK29 can induce CA overproduction to a level comparable to the Δlon mutant (Figure 4a, Figure 4—figure supplement 1), and neither the Δlon nor the ΔrcsA mutant responds to light (Figure 4a).
evidence: This is directly supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4a.

claim: Green light exposure extends worm lifespan compared to red light exposure in worms bearing MVK29.
source: We found that green light exposure extends worm lifespan compared to red light exposure (Figure 4b).
evidence: This is directly supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4b.

claim: The extent of lifespan extension at high green light intensity is 1.7-fold higher than that at low intensity.
source: Furthermore, the extent of lifespan extension at high green light intensity is 1.7-fold higher than that at low intensity (Figure 4b, Supplementary file 1c), suggesting a dose-dependent effect.
evidence: This is directly supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4b and Supplementary file 1c.

claim: The lifespan extension effect of MVK29 is dose-dependent.
source: Furthermore, the extent of lifespan extension at high green light intensity is 1.7-fold higher than that at low intensity (Figure 4b, Supplementary file 1c), suggesting a dose-dependent effect.
evidence: This is an inference from the observation that higher light intensity produces greater lifespan extension.

claim: The lifespan extension caused by Δlon is independent of light exposure.
source: In parallel, we measured the lifespan of worms bearing the CA-overproducing Δlon mutant and showed that the lifespan extension caused by Δlon is independent of light exposure (Figure 4c).
evidence: This is directly supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4c.

claim: The extent of lifespan extension caused by Δlon is comparable to that caused by MVK29.
source: The extent of lifespan extension caused by Δlon is comparable to that caused by MVK29 (Figure 4b,c, Supplementary file 1c), which is consistent with the result that Δlon and green-light-exposed MVK29 induce CA overproduction to a similar level (Figure 4a).
evidence: This is supported by comparison of experimental data in Figures 4b and 4c.

claim: Δlon and green-light-exposed MVK29 induce CA overproduction to a similar level.
source: The extent of lifespan extension caused by Δlon is comparable to that caused by MVK29 (Figure 4b,c, Supplementary file 1c), which is consistent with the result that Δlon and green-light-exposed MVK29 induce CA overproduction to a similar level (Figure 4a).
evidence: This is directly supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4a.

claim: The lifespan of worms bearing the ΔrcsA mutant is light-independent.
source: In addition, the lifespan of worms bearing the ΔrcsA mutant is also light-independent and is comparable to that of MVK29 worms under red light (Figure 4d, Supplementary file 1c).
evidence: This is directly supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4d.

claim: The lifespan of worms bearing the ΔrcsA mutant is comparable to that of MVK29 worms under red light.
source: In addition, the lifespan of worms bearing the ΔrcsA mutant is also light-independent and is comparable to that of MVK29 worms under red light (Figure 4d, Supplementary file 1c).
evidence: This is directly supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4d.

claim: Optogenetic control is sufficient to induce bacterial production of pro-longevity compounds and improve host health.
source: These results suggest that optogenetic control is sufficient to induce bacterial production of pro-longevity compounds and improve host health.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the lifespan extension data in Figure 4.

claim: Optogenetic control of bacterial metabolism can modulate a host-level phenotype in a dose-dependent manner, unlike administration of a bacterial mutant.
source: Unlike administration of a bacterial mutant, optogenetic control of bacterial metabolism can modulate a host-level phenotype in a dose-dependent manner.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from comparing the dose-dependent effects of MVK29 to the fixed effects of Δlon.

claim: About two dozen E. coli genes unrelated to CA biosynthesis enhance worm longevity when knocked out.
source: For example, we have identified about two dozen additional E. coli genes that are unrelated to CA biosynthesis and that enhance worm longevity when knocked out (Han et al., 2017), though the mechanisms by which they act remain largely unclear.
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: The mechanisms by which about two dozen E. coli genes enhance worm longevity remain largely unclear.
source: For example, we have identified about two dozen additional E. coli genes that are unrelated to CA biosynthesis and that enhance worm longevity when knocked out (Han et al., 2017), though the mechanisms by which they act remain largely unclear.
evidence: This is an assessment of the current state of knowledge based on previous work.

claim: The quorum-sensing peptide CSF and nitric oxide, both produced by Bacillus subtilis during biofilm formation, extend worm lifespan through downregulation of the insulin-like signaling pathway.
source: In another example, the quorum-sensing peptide CSF and nitric oxide, both of which are produced by Bacillus subtilis during biofilm formation, have been found to extend worm lifespan through downregulation of the insulin-like signaling pathway (Donato et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: CcaSR has been ported into B. subtilis and enables rapid and precise control of gene expression dynamics.
source: We have recently ported CcaSR into B. subtilis and demonstrated that it enables rapid and precise control of gene expression dynamics (Castillo-Hair et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: CcaSR can be co-expressed with independently-controllable blue/dark and red/far-red reversible light sensors to achieve simultaneous and independent control of the expression of up to three genes in the same bacterial cell.
source: Specifically, we and others have co-expressed CcaSR with independently-controllable blue/dark and red/far-red reversible light sensors to achieve simultaneous and independent control of the expression of up to three genes in the same bacterial cell (Fernandez-Rodriguez et al., 2017; Olson et al., 2017; Tabor et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: A large number of eukaryotic photoreceptors have been developed, enabling optical control of many cell- and neurobiological processes.
source: A large number of eukaryotic photoreceptors have also been developed, enabling optical control of many cell- and neurobiological processes (Deisseroth, 2015; Gautier et al., 2014; Goglia and Toettcher, 2019; Leopold et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: E. coli is an important model of Gram-negative bacteria.
source: Although E. coli is an important model of Gram-negative bacteria, it is not a natural symbiont of C. elegans.
evidence: This is established knowledge about E. coli.

claim: E. coli is not a natural symbiont of C. elegans.
source: Although E. coli is an important model of Gram-negative bacteria, it is not a natural symbiont of C. elegans.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the relationship between E. coli and C. elegans.

claim: E. coli does not stably colonize in the C. elegans gut.
source: Because E. coli does not stably colonize in the C. elegans gut, we have to paralyze worms to facilitate longer-term experiments.
evidence: This is based on knowledge about E. coli-C. elegans interactions and explains the experimental design.

claim: Worms must be paralyzed to facilitate longer-term experiments with E. coli.
source: Because E. coli does not stably colonize in the C. elegans gut, we have to paralyze worms to facilitate longer-term experiments.
evidence: This is an explanation of the experimental design based on the biology of the system.

claim: Light can be used to control gut bacterial gene expression in other model hosts such as flies, zebrafish, or mammals.
source: Moreover, it is likely that light can also be used to control gut bacterial gene expression in other model hosts such as flies, zebrafish, or mammals.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about potential future applications.

claim: Red-shifted wavelengths and corresponding optogenetic tools may prove superior for less optically transparent or larger animals.
source: Red-shifted wavelengths and corresponding optogenetic tools (Ong et al., 2018; Ryu and Gomelsky, 2014) may prove superior for less optically transparent or larger animals.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about potential future applications, supported by citations to relevant tools.

claim: Optogenetics will greatly improve our understanding of a wide range of microbe-host interactions.
source: Overall, by enabling precision control of bacterial gene expression and metabolism in situ, we believe that optogenetics will greatly improve our understanding of a wide range of microbe-host interactions.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about the future impact of the technology.

claim: Intestinal bacteria alter their gene expression and metabolism through aiding the digestion of ingested food and can consequently generate specific metabolites to influence other microbes and the host in close proximity.
source: In particular, through aiding the digestion of ingested food, intestinal bacteria alter their gene expression and metabolism and can consequently generate specific metabolites to influence other microbes and the host in close proximity.
evidence: This is based on general knowledge about gut microbe-host interactions.

claim: Understanding dynamic diet-microbe-host interplays demands a quantitative method to manipulate bacterial gene expression in a temporally controlled manner.
source: Understanding dynamic diet-microbe-host interplays demands a quantitative method to manipulate bacterial gene expression in a temporally controlled manner.
evidence: This is an inference about what is needed to study these complex interactions.

claim: Optogenetic approaches are quantitative, have rapid and reversible switching ability, and are suitable for in vivo application.
source: Given their quantitative nature, rapid and reversible switching ability, and suitability for in vivo application, optogenetic approaches will provide a new toolbox for this area of research to decipher how mechanistically microbial genetic factors participate in those diet-microbe-host interplays and contribute to host health and diseases.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data and properties of optogenetic systems demonstrated in the manuscript.

claim: CcaSR v2.0 exhibits 77-fold dynamic range in the reference strain BW29655 (ΔenvZ, ΔompR).
source: We note that CcaSR v2.0 exhibits 77-fold dynamic range in the reference strain BW29655 (ΔenvZ, ΔompR), which is similar to our previous measurement of this strain at 120-fold (Schmidl et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1e.

claim: CcaSR v2.0 dynamic range increases slightly to 84.2-fold in ∆rcsA (JW1935-1) due to higher sfGFP expression in green light.
source: CcaSR v2.0 dynamic range increases slightly to 84.2-fold in ∆rcsA (JW1935-1), which is used throughout this work, due to higher sfGFP expression in green light.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1e.

claim: The mCherry cassette in pLH401 decreases dynamic range to 38.3-fold due to higher leaky sfGFP expression in red light.
source: The mCherry cassette in pLH401 decreases dynamic range to 38.3-fold due to higher leaky sfGFP expression in red light.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1e.

claim: In worms, the fold-change in response to green light for pLH401 decreases to 5.52 ± 2.4 fold.
source: In worms, the fold-change in response to green light decreases further to 5.52 ± 2.4 fold (Figure 1d).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1d.

claim: The use of gfpmut3* in pLH405 decreases dynamic range to 13.5 ± 0.0 fold.
source: The use of gfpmut3* in pLH405 further decreases dynamic range to 13.5 ± 0.0 fold for reasons that are not clear, while in worms the fold-change is 8.63 ± 3.6 fold (Figure 1e).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1e.

claim: In worms, the fold-change for pLH405 is 8.63 ± 3.6 fold.
source: The use of gfpmut3* in pLH405 further decreases dynamic range to 13.5 ± 0.0 fold for reasons that are not clear, while in worms the fold-change is 8.63 ± 3.6 fold (Figure 1e).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1e.

claim: Bacterial cells outside the worm gut do not respond to light in M9Ce+Lev media conditions.
source: To demonstrate that bacterial cells outside the worm gut (e.g. on the exterior of the worm) do not respond to light in these conditions, samples of pre-conditioned bacteria from the NGM plates were suspended in the M9Ce+Lev or E. coli M9 media supplemented with casamino acids and glucose (M9Ec).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 4.

claim: Bacterial populations are only responsive to light when grown in M9Ec and when the PCB operon is intact.
source: As expected, the bacterial populations are only responsive to light when grown in M9Ec and when the PCB operon is intact (strain JW1935-1/pLH405/pSR43.6, aka LH03).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 4.

claim: The responses shown in flow cytometry data are not due to bacteria outside the worm, nor to bacteria that escape the worm over the course of the experiment.
source: We conclude that the responses shown in data in Figure 1e–f and Figure 1—figure supplement 3 are not due to bacteria outside the worm, nor to bacteria that escape the worm over the course of the experiment, as such cells do not respond to light in the experimental buffer (M9Ce).
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the control experiments in Figure 1—figure supplement 4.

claim: Levamisole has an inhibitory effect on mitochondrial NADH-oxidizing enzymes.
source: Unexpectedly, we found that 6 hr of levamisole treatment does not kill worms but leads to mitochondrial hyper-fragmentation in the intestine (Figure 3c,e), possibly due to the inhibitory effect of levamisole on mitochondrial NADH-oxidizing enzymes (Köhler and Bachmann, 1978) and its associated mitochondrial stress.
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: E. coli OP50 produces approximately 50% more CA during normal growth than BW25113.
source: The common strain E. coli OP50 was not used for worm feeding, as it produces approximately 50% more CA during normal growth than BW25113 (Han et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: Colanic acid is the only exopolysaccharide produced in the E. coli strains used that incorporates fucose.
source: We adapted a previous CA quantification protocol (Dische, 1947; Dische and Shettles, 1948) that takes advantage of the fact that it is the only exopolysaccharide produced in our E. coli strains that incorporates fucose.
evidence: This is based on knowledge about E. coli exopolysaccharide biosynthesis and supported by citations to the assay method.

claim: The sqt-3(e2117) temperature sensitive mutant reproduces normally but is embryonically lethal at 26°C.
source: To reach this goal, the sqt-3(e2117) temperature sensitive mutant (Supplementary file 1b) was used to perform longitudinal analyses at 25°C, which avoids time-consuming animal transfer without interrupting normal reproduction. sqt-3(e2117) is a collagen mutant of C. elegans that reproduces normally but is embryonically lethal at 26°C and has been used previously in longitudinal studies (Han et al., 2017; Wang et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.
